items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: You never heard that sort of thing from people like Gene Krupa.

ctx.x: It was generally known among musicians that France was less prejudiced than America, and that life was generally easier for black musicians. However, I never gave that a thought at the time. The prejudice in the United States was not something that worried me. I don't think musicians paid as much attention to those things as a teacher or a lawyer, or someone with a different sort of education. Musicians travelled around and they knew what was happening - they knew that there was prejudice, not only in the South,…

As far as prejudice from other white musicians was concerned, this was mainly confined to the bad musicians who could not get a good job. You never heard that sort of thing from people like Gene Krupa. Even though blacks and whites belonged to the same union, they could not earn the same salaries, and even if a black orchestra got a job in a downtown district, they got paid less. It was a rotten system, but one which left the black musicians freer, to play their own music.
When we set sail for France, Carol Dickerson of Chicago came to see us off, as he was a friend of Eugene Anderson, the ex-Cooper pianist. Most of the musicians in Lucky's band had been with Cooper.
